California Influenza Adjusted Deaths

Data Sources

This analysis draws on four California-specific and national data sources:

  • NHSN hospitalization data ( CDC NHSN Hospital Respiratory Data ) offers near-universal, mandatory, lab-confirmed influenza hospitalization counts reported by California facilities, though only at a coarse 4-group age resolution (<5, 5-17, 18-64, 65+).
  • CA death certificate data provides California-specific influenza-coded deaths with full age and geographic detail, though influenza is chronically underlisted as a cause of death.
  • FluSurv-NET ( CDC FluView Interactive — FluSurv-NET Hospitalization Rates; data accessible via FluView GRASP) supplies weekly, age-stratified (7-group) hospitalization rates per 100,000 catchment population from CDC’s Emerging Infections Program surveillance network, with a Northern California catchment spanning Alameda, Contra Costa, and San Francisco counties — the same underlying system CDC uses to build its national flu burden estimates, making it directly comparable to CDC’s published adjustment ratios. These are supplemented by two national reference tables:
  • CDC’s flu disease burden model inputs ( Estimated US Flu Disease Burden Dashboard), providing national hospitalization under-detection adjustments and death-to-hospitalization ratios by age/season.
  • NCHS national mortality surveillance ( NCHS Mortality Surveillance System, P&I/Influenza Mortality), providing national influenza-coded death totals, available only from the 2018-19 season forward and only at the all-ages level.

Methods

Method 1 (National multipliers) extrapolates CA’s FluSurv-NET hospitalization rate to the statewide population, calibrates it against actual NHSN hospitalization counts (to correct for the fact that the EIP catchment may not perfectly represent the rest of the state), and then applies CDC’s national hospitalization under-detection adjustment and death-to-hospitalization ratio to arrive at estimated deaths. This methodology roughly follows the flu burden cascade process outlined in Reed et al. (2015).

Method 1 (CA multipliers) follows an identical hospitalization-extrapolation pathway, but substitutes CDC’s national under-detection adjustment with a CA-specific adjustment built from state testing-sensitivity and testing-proportion data (provided by the CDC), weighted by implied FluSurv-NET hospitalization volume.

Method 2 (Death-certificate scaling) takes an entirely different approach: it reconstructs CDC’s implied national under-ascertainment multiplier (the ratio of CDC’s nationally estimated deaths to NCHS’s nationally reported flu-coded deaths) and applies that multiplier directly to California’s own observed flu-coded death certificates, scaling up CA’s real death-certificate counts rather than working forward from hospitalizations at all.

Key Assumptions and Limitations

Method 1 (both variations) assumes that age-specific hospitalization rates observed in the Northern California EIP catchment counties are representative of statewide rates — a standard assumption in CDC’s own national methodology, but one that may not hold if testing practices, care-seeking behavior, or population risk factors differ meaningfully between the catchment counties and the rest of California. Because the two data sources use incompatible age schemes (FluSurv-NET’s 7 groups vs. NHSN’s 4), hospitalization counts had to be re-aggregated to a common scheme before calibration, and the calibration ratio itself was found to stabilize only toward the end of each season — so season-total (rather than week-specific) calibration ratios were used, with a cross-season mean as a fallback for seasons lacking sufficient data.

The CA-multiplier variation additionally depends on how its underlying sensitivity/testing-proportion data are weighted when aggregating across age groups; the most defensible approach (weighting by implied hospitalization volume) was used where possible, falling back to population-weighting or an unweighted mean where volume data were unavailable — meaning the CA-specific adjustment carries uncertainty that is likely understated by point estimates alone.

Method 2 depends entirely on the national multiplier (CDC-estimated deaths ÷ NCHS-coded deaths) being a reasonable proxy for California’s own true under-ascertainment and is further constrained by lack of age stratification, which required collapsing CDC’s age-specific estimates to an all-ages total before the multiplier could be constructed. Across all three methods, no uncertainty intervals are currently propagated beyond what’s directly observable in the input data, since CDC’s public burden-model inputs are point estimates only.

Uncertainty Propagation and Ensemble Methodology

To move beyond point estimates, we propagated uncertainty through each of the three estimation approaches using a bootstrap and Monte Carlo simulation framework, then combined the results into a pooled ensemble. Rather than treating the various adjustment ratios (hospitalization under-detection, death-to-hospitalization ratios, NHSN-FluSurv-NET calibration ratios, and the national death-certificate scaling multiplier) as fixed constants, we modeled each as a distribution built from the historical spread of season- and age-specific values. For seasons and age groups with their own directly observed ratio, we used a weighted-anchor bootstrap that draws predominantly (70% of the time) from that season’s own value while still drawing occasionally from the broader historical observed values. Seasons lacking season-specific data draw entirely from the pooled historical spread resulting in a wider sampling that reflects genuine uncertainty. Observed hospitalization and death counts themselves were treated using a Gamma-Poisson posterior (rather than as exact fixed values or standard Poisson sampling), which avoids an artificial collapse to zero-width intervals in sparse pediatric age groups (<5, 5-17) where weekly counts are frequently zero but true underlying risk is not. We also identified and excluded a small number of observed edge cases — namely, two CDC-reported death-to-hospitalization ratios of exactly zero for pediatric age groups in the 2011-12 (historically mild season) and 2021-22 seasons (overlapping with COVID pandemic including school closures and NPIs). California’s own death-certificate data confirms non-zero pediatric flu mortality in all recent seasons for which data are available.

Each method’s ratios were combined multiplicatively across hundreds of simulated draws to produce a full distribution of plausible weekly and season-total death estimates for Method 1 (both national- and CA-multiplier variants) and Method 2. To arrive at a single combined estimate, we used a pooled ensemble approach: all simulated draws from the three methods are concatenated into one distribution at each season/age-group, and the median and 95% interval are taken directly from that pooled set. This approach is intentionally conservative — it reflects both the within-method statistical uncertainty and the across-method disagreement simultaneously, without assuming the three methods are independent (since all three ultimately rely on shared CDC-derived inputs somewhere in their respective chains). An inverse-variance weighted ensemble, which down-weights methods with wider individual uncertainty, was also computed as a sensitivity check but is not used as the primary reported estimate, given the likely correlation between methods. Taken together, this framework allows us to report not just a single “best guess” of California’s influenza death burden, but a defensible range that reflects genuine data limitations — including thin historical reporting, known data artifacts, and irreducible disagreement between independent estimation strategies.
